records.text: Fork. A single piece now hits several targets, and one reply rarely rescues all of them.
This permits a fork. One enemy piece can now attack several targets with a single move; pinpoint it first.
A fork was available in the stronger move, one piece striking several targets in a single move. Unused here.
Absolute pin. The pinned piece has no legal exit from the line while its king stands behind it.
This concedes an absolute pin. The pinned piece is fixed on its line; moving it off would be illegal.
The stronger move pinned an enemy piece to its king. This move leaves that piece free to move.
Skewer. The front piece must move off the line, and the piece behind it becomes a target.
This concedes a skewer. Once the front piece is driven off the line, the piece behind it can be taken.
The stronger move set up a skewer: attack the front piece, collect the one behind it. Unused here.
Defender eliminated. Whatever depended on that piece for protection is now exposed.
One defender can now be captured. If it goes, the piece it guards loses that protection.
The stronger move captured a defender and stripped the protection from the piece behind it. This move leaves the defender in place.
Back-rank mating motif. The king's own pieces block its escape squares, and the rank behind it is the weakness.
This permits a back-rank mate. The king has no escape square in front of it, and the last rank is the weakness.
Back-rank mate was on offer: the enemy king's own pieces blocked its exits. Not exploited.
The pawn advances toward promotion. Each step narrows the defense.
This gives an enemy pawn a path toward promotion. Track it square by square; each advance changes the requirements of the defense.
The stronger move pushed a pawn closer to promotion. Here, that pawn stays put.
Discovered attack. The front piece moves, and the piece behind it attacks down the line that just opened.
This concedes a discovered attack. One enemy piece masks another; when the front piece moves, the rear piece attacks along the cleared line.
The stronger move contained a discovered attack: move the front piece, open the line for the one behind. Not used here.
Double attack. Two targets are threatened by one move, and a single reply rarely meets both.
This permits a double attack. A single enemy move can now create two threats, each requiring its own response.
The stronger move generated two simultaneous threats. The played move lacks that double threat.
Deflection. The defender is pulled away from its task, and the piece or square it covered is left unguarded.
Deflection risk created. One defender can now be drawn off its duty; identify what it currently covers.
The stronger move deflected a defender from its duty. This move leaves the defense intact.
Unprotected piece captured; there is no recapture.
An unprotected piece was available for capture with the stronger move. Check for undefended targets before quiet moves.
A piece is now unprotected, and the other side can capture it without a recapture.
This move abandons a defense. The piece's only defender relocates, and the piece can now be captured.
The opponent's last move posed a direct threat. This reply leaves it unmet, and a piece remains capturable.
The capture is incomplete as a calculation. The recapture removes a higher-value piece, so the exchange loses material.
Development counted: a minor piece is now active, off its original square.
The alternative brought a minor piece off its starting square. Here, development waits.
The rook's file is fully open now, with no pawn of either color on it.
The alternative put a rook on a fully open file.
Rook file status: semi-open. No friendly pawns, one or more enemy pawns.
The alternative put a rook on a semi-open file, without friendly pawns but with enemy pawns present.
Passed pawn established. Ahead of it, on its own file and both adjacent files, there is no enemy pawn.
The alternative produced a passed pawn, unopposed by enemy pawns on its file and both flanking files.
The passed pawn advances one step closer to promotion.
The alternative advanced the passed pawn. Here it stays on its square.
Isolated pawn created. Both adjacent files are empty of friendly pawns.
The alternative left a pawn isolated, its adjacent files empty of friendly pawns.
A previously unprotected piece now has a defender.
The alternative added a defender to a piece that currently has none.
Defender count for one piece is now zero. Zero defenders is a weakness, not by itself a loss.
The alternative left a piece without its last defender. That alone would not have established a loss.
The king now has one more legal flight square. Identify which piece movement cleared it.
The alternative opened one more legal flight square for the king. Identify which move would have cleared it.
Castled. The king moves two squares, and the rook relocates beside it in the same move.
Castling was available. King and rook would have relocated in one move.
The bishop pair no longer exists after this capture. Only one square color remains covered by that side's bishops.
The alternative captured a bishop and broke the opposing bishop pair.
Doubled pawns. A single file carries two same-colored pawns.
The alternative produced doubled pawns, with two of one color sharing a file.
Forced mate for the other side, starting now. Trace the attack back to the first defensive concession.
A mating line was available and went unplayed. Locate it afterward.
Sound sacrifice. Taking the material is allowed, and the checked line still justifies the offer.
Only move. The rest of the examined candidates lose, and the position stays playable through this one.
Of all the examined candidates, only this move keeps the advantage. Exact.
Material can be taken by the other side on the very next move. Address it first.
For the other side, the strongest reply gives check. King safety takes priority over every other consideration.
Another move is preferred by the engine. Compare both against the strongest reply.
This concedes value against the engine's best option. The reply shows where the loss occurs.
Strong. Among the moves examined, very little value is conceded.
Sound. The bulk of the position's value is retained, though the engine ranks another move first.
High natural rating from the human-move model. A stronger move exists in the engine's search, and the reply demonstrates the cost.
Unlikely, on the human-move model's scale. Engine verdict: strong. Unconventional, and correct.
A single move held the position, and the human-move model scores that defense as hard to locate. Study it.
Difficult to find: that is the rating from the human-move model and from the searched alternatives. Precise.
The position held. Both the human-move model and the searched alternatives classify this defense as difficult. Correctly found.
Natural, by the human-move model's rating. Best, by the engine's search. Both agree.
High natural rating from the human-move model. Engine: strong. Top move: another.
Played with very little time on the clock.
Played quickly, with a substantial time reserve remaining.
A long think on the clock before this move.
The theory catalogue includes this move.
Opening theory stops at this point. From here on, no prepared line applies.
Playable again despite the earlier error. That is the correct repair.
The position is playable again after the earlier error, with assistance from the other side's mistakes.
The opponent's last move conceded a concrete opportunity, and this move takes full advantage.
The opponent's last move conceded a concrete opportunity. This reply lets it pass; a stronger answer existed.
Recurrence: this issue already appeared earlier in the game. Compare the instances; the shared pattern is the lesson.
A piece that lost its protection earlier is defended again. Compare the position before and after.
Several small concessions have accumulated, and this move is one more. Individually minor; together significant.
The advantage was converted through to the recorded win without being returned. Technically clean.
Other saved games contain the same issue. Review them together to isolate the pattern.
Checkmate. The king has no legal move; game over.
Checkmate. Every square for the defending king is covered or occupied. Review the decisions that preceded it.
Draw. The result cannot change; the decisions that produced it remain worth reviewing.
Assess the position. Select a move when the calculation is complete.
Incorrect. Recalculate and select again.
The attempt returned no result. Submit the move again.
The saved engine analysis records a forced mate in favor of the side that played this move.
The saved engine analysis finds that this move concedes a forced checkmate against its own side.
Net result of the saved line: the side that played this move finishes ahead in material.
Net result of the saved line: the side that played this move finishes behind in material.
Accepted by the exercise. No clear tactical reason appears in the moves shown, and none will be invented.
Not accepted by the exercise. No clear tactical reason is visible in the moves shown. Reassess the position from the start.
Exact match with a saved answer. In this exercise, the saved answers define correctness.
Outside the exercise's saved answers. A legal move outside them may still be objectively sound.
Review the move and the reason for it, then continue to the next position.
Correct. Retain the reason; the reason transfers to other positions, the move does not.
Attempt logged. No change to the review dates.
Solved. The relearning status on this recall remains in effect for now.
Starting position, before any move in this line.
Next move. Register what it changes.
Check. The king must be addressed before anything else.
The check is resolved.
Promotion: the pawn is exchanged for a new piece on the last rank.
The pawn promotes, and check comes from the new piece.
The pawn promotes with checkmate. No legal king move remains.
The pawn promotes, and the promotion also resolves the check on its own king.
Capture. Material leaves the board.
Check, delivered by a capture. Material and tempo in one move.
Capture with checkmate. Game over.
Capture, and the king is out of check in the same move.
A pawn capture lands on the last rank, and the pawn promotes.
The pawn captures, promotes, and checks with the new piece.
The pawn captures, promotes, and delivers checkmate.
Capture plus promotion, and its own king is out of check in the same move.
Castling, and check from the same move.
Castling delivers checkmate. Zero legal replies.
Mechanism of the fork: a single attacker hits several targets and collects one. In this example, the net material balance also improves.
Absolute pin on this piece. The marked capture is illegal, because leaving the line would expose the king.
Pinned to its king, the attacked piece may only move along the line that keeps the king covered.
No defender can recapture, because every one of them is pinned to its king. That is the mechanism behind the capture, and the line shown finishes with a material gain.
The pinned piece cannot leave the line its king stands behind, and it is captured before the sequence ends.
Forced off the line, the front piece abandons the one behind, which is captured.
Check compels the king to leave the line, and the same attacker collects what stood behind it.
Sequence: capture the only defender, then take what it was protecting.
Pulled off its post, the defender abandons the piece it covered, and that piece falls.
The blocking piece moves, the line opens, and the rear piece captures along it.
A piece moves off the line, and the opened line gives check.
Double check. Two pieces give check at once, so only a king move is legal.
The moving piece attacks one target; the line it opens attacks a second. The rear attacker collects its target.
Promotion achieved. At the end of this example, that side is also ahead in material overall.
An unprotected piece is captured. The capturing side finishes this example ahead in material.
The attacking piece was held by a relative pin. The opponent's previous move released it, and it now captures a target that did not move, in the line shown.
The marked reply is a legal option. Play it on the board and examine the result.
Before moving, verify that no piece can be captured without an adequate recapture.
Before any quiet move, check every enemy piece for missing protection.
Among the forcing moves, test for a single piece hitting two valuable targets.
Before moving a pinned piece, establish what stands behind it, whether king or higher-value piece.
Check the line behind the first target. A more valuable piece may be standing there.
Before exchanging a defender, list what it defends.
When a piece leaves a line, check what that line now attacks.
Look for single moves that create two threats, including checks and newly opened lines.
Before moving a back-rank defender, confirm the king retains an escape square.
Count the squares a pawn needs to promote. Identify which pawn advances require an answer.
Before moving a defender, list the pieces that rely on it.
Before capturing, compare the value gained with what the recapture takes back.
Test whether a forcing exchange overloads a defender with a second duty.
This exercise grades only against its saved answers. A legal move outside them can still be sound.
The line is shown against strong replies. They are not necessarily the only replies.
Material changes are counted within the line shown, measured from where that line starts. The written explanation states which piece values apply.
No simple tactical reason appears in the saved line, and no positional reason will be guessed. Work through it and test each reply yourself.
This explanation is governed by the answer policy saved with the exercise. For that setting, consult the written notes.
The opening line, move by move, in order.
Correct. That move is part of the study material.
Select the next move from the opening lines under study.
More than one chosen opening line applies here. Any of them supplies a valid move.
Recall the next move from the study material.
The chosen opening lines do not contain that move. Try again.
Outside the chosen lines; try again. The study has changed, so this saved attempt does not alter review dates.
Outside the chosen lines; try again. The position is retired, and its review dates are fixed.
Under Mixed Due, any move from this line is accepted. Dedicated practice requires this line specifically.
Due recalls will request the moves for the chosen side. Several active studies sharing one position produce a single card for it.
Before the next move, reload the saved session.
Verified line, now playing on the board.
Recorded as revealed. The solution remains available below.
Solved on a later attempt. The record keeps the earlier miss alongside the solution.
Solved without an error. Every move correct.
Incorrect for this puzzle. Previous correct moves stay saved.
Correct. Next move.
Calculate fully. Move when the line is clear.
The engine analysis is insufficient to explain this position. No guess will be offered.
Review paused. Resume below, or test a move on the board.
Select a move to review, or test a move on the board.
Opening theory begins here. This move has a catalogue entry.
Theory move; a known opening lists it.
This move has its own recorded entry in opening theory.
Theory continues.
This move is covered by theory as well.
The reply has a catalogue entry too.
Still within the book line.
Listed in theory.
No deviation from theory.
Theory again.
Book move. Being in theory locates the game; it does not evaluate the move.
High natural rating from the human-move model. It hands the other side a forced mate. Trace the attack back to the first defensive concession.
A mating line was available. This move, natural by the human-move model's rating, leaves it unplayed. Check for mate first when the king is exposed.
Natural by the human-move model's prediction, but it permits an immediate capture. Read the reply before anything else.
High natural rating from the human-move model. The engine prefers another move, and the reply shows exactly what is conceded.
Natural by the human-move model's rating, but it permits a fork: one enemy piece can attack several targets. Identify that piece.
High natural rating from the human-move model. It permits a skewer; the front piece is driven off, and the piece behind it falls.
The only searched move that keeps the position playable, and the human-move model rates this defense difficult. Located under pressure.
Every other examined move loses, and the game stays playable only through this one. Rated a difficult find by the human-move model, ranked top by the engine. Precisely located.
Only this move retains the advantage; every other examined move loses. Human-move model rating for this resource: difficult. Located.
The advantage is retained by this move and no other; every other examined move loses. Engine ranking: first. Human-move model and searched alternatives: difficult to locate.
Fork, with multiple targets under one attacker. Human-move model: unlikely. Engine: strong. The low prediction does not reduce its value.
A hidden fork. Several targets, a single attacker. Best in the engine's search, and rated difficult by the human-move model. Correctly found.
Absolute pin. The piece cannot legally leave its line. Rated improbable by the human-move model, rated strong by the engine.
Absolute pin, fixing the piece on its line. Low probability per the human-move model, first place per the engine. A difficult resource, located.
The human-move model rates this natural, but the piece's only defender relocates, and the piece can now be captured.
The sole defender moves away; the guarded piece is now capturable. One searched move, and only one, would have kept the position. Difficulty rating from the human-move model: high.
The opponent's last move posed a direct threat. This reply, natural by the human-move model's prediction, leaves it unmet, and a piece remains capturable.
The threat from the opponent's last move stands, and a piece remains capturable after this move. The only holding defense was another move, and the human-move model classifies it as hard to find.
High natural rating from the human-move model for the capture. The recapture removes a higher-value piece, so the exchange loses material.
Recapture of higher value follows. Net loss. A single searched defense held, and its human-move model rating marks it as hidden. Study it.
Fork. One piece attacks several targets with one move. The human-move model rates it natural, and the engine's search confirms it as the top move. No discrepancy.
Several targets, now under attack from one piece. Natural, by the human-move model's prediction. Engine: strong. Top move: another.
This permits a fork against several targets. The position required one specific defense, which the human-move model scores as difficult to locate.
The stronger move contained a fork. This move, natural by the human-move model's rating, does not use it.
The holding defense contained a fork. Unplayed. Human-move model rating for that defense: difficult.
Absolute pin: the piece shields its king and cannot step aside. Natural by prediction, best by calculation. The two measurements coincide.
A piece is now pinned in front of its king. Human-move model: high natural rating. Engine: strong, with its top pick elsewhere.
Natural by the human-move model's prediction, but it concedes an absolute pin; the pinned piece loses its freedom of movement.
After this move, a pin against the king is available to the other side. Among the searched moves, a single one kept the position, and the human-move model gives it a low chance of being found.
The stronger move pinned an enemy piece to its king. This move, which the human-move model rates natural, leaves that piece free.
The holding defense pinned a piece to its king. Unplayed. Few players would locate that defense, per the human-move model.
Skewer. The front piece moves, and what stood behind it is open to capture. The engine's top move, which the human-move model and the searched alternatives classify as hard to see.
Skewer, from an unexpected angle. The front piece has to give way. The human-move model gives it a low probability; the engine's verdict is strong all the same.
Once the front piece yields, the piece behind it is open to capture. Intuition and calculation give the same answer here: high natural rating, top engine ranking.
Skewer: front piece attacked, rear piece behind it. On the human-move model's list of likely moves. Engine assessment: strong; preferred move: a different one.
This concedes a skewer: front piece driven off, rear piece exposed. The holding move was elsewhere, and the human-move model rates that defense difficult. Note it.
The stronger move set a skewer on the line. This move, natural by the human-move model's prediction, leaves it unplayed.
The holding defense included a skewer along the line. Unplayed. Human-move model rating for that defense: difficult.
Defender eliminated. Its protection is gone. Rated hard to find by the human-move model, ranked best by the engine. Exact work.
A defender is captured, and the piece it covered is exposed. Low on the human-move model's scale, sound on the engine's.
Remove the defender; the protected piece becomes a target. A high natural rating from the human-move model; nothing in the engine's search ranks above it.
This removes a defender from the board. Rated natural by prediction and strong by calculation. The engine's own pick is a different move.
Natural by the human-move model's prediction. Now one defender is capturable, and the piece it covers would lose protection.
A defender is now capturable, and the piece it covers would be exposed. One searched move, and only one, would have kept the position. Difficulty rating from the human-move model: high.
The stronger move captured a defender. This move, natural per the human-move model, leaves that defender on duty.
The holding defense captured a defender and exposed the piece behind it. Human-move model rating for that defense: difficult.
Back-rank motif. Own pieces block every exit square of the king. The human-move model gives it little chance of being found. Engine verdict: best. Found.
Back-rank idea. The king has no flight square off the last rank. Few players would choose it, by the human-move model's estimate. Engine verdict: strong.
The weakness is the back rank; the king's own pieces seal it in. Prediction and calculation select the same move here. Intuition verified by search.
A back-rank mating pattern forms. Predicted with high confidence by the human-move model. Engine verdict: strong, with a different top move.
The pawn advances toward promotion. Each step narrows the defense. First in the engine's ranking, and a difficult find by the human-move model's rating.
A pawn begins its advance toward promotion. Low prediction from the human-move model, strong evaluation from the engine. Unconventional and correct.
The pawn moves closer to promotion. High natural rating from the human-move model, first place in the engine's ranking.
A pawn steps closer to the promotion rank. Anticipated by the human-move model. The engine accepts it as strong, with its preference elsewhere.
The human-move model rates this natural, but an enemy pawn now has a route to promotion. Track it square by square.
An enemy pawn now has a route to promotion. The only holding defense was another move, and the human-move model classifies it as hard to find.
The stronger move pushed a pawn closer to promotion. This move, natural by the human-move model's prediction, leaves it in place.
The holding defense advanced a pawn toward promotion. Unplayed. By the human-move model's rating, a defense few would locate.
The front piece moves, and the rear piece attacks along the opened line. The engine prefers it to every alternative, while the human-move model and the searched moves classify it as a difficult find.
Discovered attack. The masking piece steps away. Outside the human-move model's predictions; inside the engine's strong range.
The line opens, and the piece behind attacks down it. The human-move model anticipates this move, and the engine finds no improvement on it.
Discovered attack along the cleared line. High natural rating from the human-move model; strong on the engine's assessment, not its top selection.
Natural by the human-move model's prediction, but it permits a discovered attack: an enemy piece masks another, ready to open the line.
Discovered attack now possible for the other side. A single searched defense held, and its human-move model rating marks it as hidden. Study it.
A discovered attack was available in the stronger move. This move, natural by the human-move model's prediction, keeps the line closed.
The holding defense opened a line for a discovered attack. Unplayed. Human-move model rating for that defense: hidden.
Double attack. One move, two targets. Hard to find on the human-move model's scale, top choice on the engine's. Both measurements stand.
Two simultaneous threats from this move. Off the human-move model's predicted path, and strong by the engine's search all the same.
Two targets threatened by a single move. Anticipated by the human-move model and unimproved upon in the engine's search.
Double attack; each threat needs its own answer. Expected by the human-move model and rated strong by the engine, whose top choice is another move.
The human-move model rates this natural, but a single enemy move can now create two threats.
One enemy move can now create two threats. The position required one specific defense, which the human-move model scores as difficult to locate.
The stronger move generated two simultaneous threats. This move, natural by the human-move model's prediction, lacks that pair of threats.
The holding defense created two threats at once. Unplayed. Human-move model rating for that defense: difficult.
Deflection. The defender is pulled from its post. Rated a difficult find by the human-move model, ranked top by the engine. Precisely located.
The defender is pulled off its assignment. Improbable as a human choice, per the model. Strong as an engine choice.
Pull the defender away; what it covered is left unguarded. Two measures, one verdict: natural to the human-move model, number one to the engine.
Deflection of a defender from its duty. Natural in human-move terms, strong in engine terms. The engine's preferred move is another one.
Natural by the human-move model's rating, but one defender can now be drawn off its duty, and what it covers would be exposed.
One defender is now vulnerable to deflection. Among the searched moves, a single one kept the position, and the human-move model gives it a low chance of being found.
The stronger move deflected a defender. This move, natural by the human-move model's prediction, leaves that defender undisturbed.
The holding defense deflected a defender from its duty. Unplayed; the human-move model scores that defense as hidden.
An unprotected piece is captured. No recapture. Engine ranking: first. Human-move model and searched alternatives: difficult to locate.
Unprotected piece taken, by an unexpected route. An unexpected move by the human-move model's measure, and strong by the engine's calculation.
Undefended, and captured. Natural move, best move. The human-move model and the engine concur.
Capture of an undefended piece. Natural and strong, by the two measures. The engine's first choice is a different move.
An unprotected piece was available with the stronger move. This move, natural by the human-move model's rating, does not take it.
The holding defense captured an unprotected piece. Unplayed. Human-move model rating for that defense: difficult.
The human-move model rates this natural, but it leaves a piece unprotected, and the other side can capture it.
A piece is left unprotected and capturable. The holding move was elsewhere, and the human-move model rates that defense difficult. Note it.
Minor piece developed. Best in the engine's search, and rated difficult by the human-move model. Correctly found. A quiet move, and still a difficult one.
One minor piece is now active. Human-move model: unlikely. Engine: strong. The low prediction does not reduce its value.
Development: a minor piece enters play. The human-move model rates it natural, and the engine's search confirms it as the top move. No discrepancy.
One more minor piece is active. Natural, by the human-move model's prediction. Engine grade: strong. Top move: another.
Rook to a file with zero pawns on it. Low probability per the human-move model, first place per the engine. A difficult resource, located.
Fully open file, now occupied by the rook. Rated improbable by the human-move model, rated strong by the engine.
Open file: rook installed. Natural by prediction, best by calculation. The two measurements coincide.
A rook now controls the open file. Human-move model: high natural rating. Search evaluation: strong, with its top pick elsewhere.
The rook's file: semi-open, its own pawns absent, enemy pawns present. The engine's top move, which the human-move model and the searched alternatives classify as hard to see.
A half-open file, now with a rook on it. The human-move model gives it a low probability; the engine's verdict is strong all the same.
Rook on the semi-open file, facing enemy pawns only. Intuition and calculation give the same answer here: high natural rating, top engine ranking.
A rook now uses a semi-open file. On the human-move model's list of likely moves. Engine assessment: strong; preferred move: a different one.
Passed pawn established: no enemy pawn ahead on its file or adjacent files. Rated hard to find by the human-move model, ranked best by the engine. Exact work.
A passed pawn is created here. Low on the human-move model's scale, sound on the engine's.
A passed pawn now exists on the board. A high natural rating from the human-move model; nothing in the engine's search ranks above it.
Passed pawn. No enemy pawn stands in its path or beside it. Rated natural by prediction and strong by calculation. The engine's own pick is a different move.
The passed pawn is one square nearer promotion. The human-move model gives it little chance of being found. Engine verdict: best. Found.
The passed pawn moves one step closer to promotion. Few players would choose it, by the human-move model's estimate. Engine assessment: strong.
Passed pawn forward. Prediction and calculation select the same move here. Intuition verified by search.
This advances the passed pawn. Natural, with high confidence, per the human-move model. Search result: strong, with a different top move.

Pawn structure now includes an isolani, both adjacent files bare of its own pawns. First in the engine's ranking, and a difficult find by the human-move model's rating. The best move can still carry a structural cost.
Structural result: one isolated pawn. Low prediction from the human-move model, strong evaluation from the engine. Unconventional and correct.
Isolated pawn created. High natural rating from the human-move model, first place in the engine's ranking.
One pawn is now isolated from its neighbors. Anticipated by the human-move model. The engine accepts it as strong, with its preference elsewhere.
A defender is assigned to a previously unprotected piece. The engine prefers it to every alternative, while the human-move model and the searched moves classify it as a difficult find.
A defender is added to an unguarded piece. Outside the human-move model's predictions; inside the engine's strong range.
The piece now has a defender. The human-move model anticipates this move, and the engine finds no improvement on it.
Protection added to a previously undefended piece. High natural rating from the human-move model; strong on the engine's assessment, not its top selection.
A piece is stripped of its defender. Weakened, not lost. Hard to find on the human-move model's scale, top choice on the engine's. Both measurements stand.
This leaves a piece undefended, which by itself does not mean it can be won. Off the human-move model's predicted path, and strong by the engine's search all the same.
Zero defenders now for one piece; no loss follows from that alone. Anticipated by the human-move model and unimproved upon in the engine's search.
Defender count for one piece: zero. Not by itself a loss. Expected by the human-move model and rated strong by the engine, whose top choice is another move.
One extra legal flight square for the king. Rated a difficult find by the human-move model, ranked top by the engine. Precisely located.
An additional legal square opens for the king. Improbable as a human choice, per the model. Strong as an engine choice. Identify which move cleared it.
The king's legal squares increase by one. Two measures, one verdict: natural to the human-move model, number one to the engine.
This gives the king one more legal square. Natural in human-move terms, strong in engine terms. The engine's preferred move is another one.
Castled. One move, two pieces placed. Engine ranking: first. Human-move model and searched alternatives: difficult to locate.
King castled; the rook lands on its far side. An unexpected move by the human-move model's measure, and strong by the engine's calculation.
Castling: king and rook, a single move. Natural move, best move. The human-move model and the engine concur.
Castling completed. Natural and strong, by the two measures. The engine's first choice is a different move.
With this capture, the opposing bishop pair no longer exists. Best in the engine's search, and rated difficult by the human-move model. Correctly found.
A bishop is captured, and the opposing pair is broken. Human-move model: unlikely. Engine grade: strong. The low prediction does not reduce its value.
After this capture, the opposing side has no bishop pair. The human-move model rates it natural, and the engine's search confirms it as the top move. No discrepancy.
The opposing side loses its bishop pair. Natural, by the human-move model's prediction. Search evaluation: strong. Top move: another.
Doubled pawns result, one behind the other on a single file. Low probability per the human-move model, first place per the engine. A difficult resource, located.
This produces doubled pawns. Rated improbable by the human-move model, rated strong by the engine.
Pawns now doubled. Natural by prediction, best by calculation. The two measurements coincide.
